articleSummary: Harvest mites (neotrombicula autumnalis) are thriving in the UK, with activity peaking in September–October as eggs hatch. These tiny six-legged parasites latch onto humans or dogs after brushing through grass and soil, inject enzymes, and feed on liquefied skin. Bites are usually invisible, with itching starting about 24 hours later and presenting as itchy red bumps (often in clusters) around the waist, ankles, and skin folds; the condition is trombiculosis. UK mites do not transmit disease, unlike scrub typhus in East Asia/South Pacific; in the USA chigger bites have been linked to summer penile syndrome. Management includes showers, antihistamines, and hydrocortisone cream; cold packs help itching. For dogs, monitor for itching and vet-check suspected infestation due to seasonal canine illness (SCI). Prevent exposure by keeping skin covered and maintaining flea prevention; treat bites early to avoid infection.

articleSummary: Kerala, India faces higher dengue fever risk linked to El Niño and climate change, with temperature and monsoon rainfall shaping transmission. A GeoHealth study using Kerala climate and dengue data from 2016–2025 finds that higher temperatures and El Niño provide 2–3 month lead indicators, while monsoon rainfall offers a near-term signal. Dengue typically rises in May, peaks in June–July, with about 60% of reported cases during the southwest monsoon. Before the monsoon, temperatures reach 30.5–32.5°C, relative humidity 66–79%, and monthly rainfall 180–450 mm—conditions favorable for spread. Very heavy rains can temporarily reduce transmission by washing away eggs and larvae. From June–August 2026, Kerala recorded 7,188 confirmed dengue cases—roughly 60% above the 2016–2025 three‑month average and over fivefold the 2006–2015 average. Projections indicate a 16–20% rise during 2021–2040 due to climate change; by century’s end, increases range from 46% (low emissions) to 113% (high emissions).

articleHeadline: Measles is making a comeback. Will we end it for good? - Phnom Penh Post
articleSummary: Measles is resurging in the Western Pacific, eroding decades of progress toward elimination. Globally, vaccination has prevented about 154 million deaths since 1974, with measles vaccination saving roughly 94 million lives (including 12 million in the Western Pacific). Outbreaks reappear as COVID-19-era disruptions and antivaccine misinformation weaken coverage, revealing immunity gaps. The region, home to 2.2 billion people, reported about 1.6 million zero-dose children in 2025. In 2024 and 2025, nearly 20 million births occurred, all needing routine immunisation. Last year, WHO certified measles and rubella elimination as a public health threat in all 21 Pacific island countries and areas, yet nine countries remain not yet eliminated: Cambodia, China, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and Vietnam. Elimination by 2030 requires renewed political commitment, robust routine immunisation and surveillance, resilient supply chains, and sustained funding, recognizing immunisation as long-term health security.

articleSummary: Endemic in Brazil, meningitis occurs year-round, with bacterial and viral forms common. Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges caused by various agents: bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae); viruses (enteroviruses, HSV, varicella-zoster, arboviruses); plus fungal and parasitic forms. Bacterial meningitis is typically the most severe; viral forms are often milder. Meningococcal disease can cause meningitis and meningococcemia, with rash, cold extremities, severe pain, and rapid breathing. Transmission varies: bacteria and some viruses via droplets; enteroviruses fecal-oral; fungi rarely spread person-to-person. Symptoms include fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, altered mental status; infants may be irritable, feed poorly, lethargic. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment with CSF and blood tests; vaccination via the National Immunization Program is the main prevention. 2026 Ceará data show 123 cases and seven deaths across 51 municipalities, indicating a return to pre-pandemic levels.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Stay vigilant against these diseases during the monsoon.
articleHeadline: बारिश में इन बीमारियों से रहें सावधान
articleSummary: Monsoon season raises infections including dengue and malaria from mosquito bites. Dengue causes high fever, headache, body aches, and pain behind the eyes; prevent by eliminating standing water around the home, using bed nets and repellents, and seeking medical care for high fever or unusual symptoms. Malaria presents with fever that may alternate with chills, sweating, and weakness; use mosquito nets and repellents as protective measures and do not ignore prolonged fever. Typhoid fever and Cholera risk increase with contaminated water and food during rains; drink only clean water, cook food thoroughly, and wash hands before meals and after using the toilet. Water from floods or dirty water can pose infection risks; avoid entering dirty water and wear rubber boots and gloves if needed. After rain, fever, muscle pain, or weakness warrants medical consultation. Enjoy the rains, but stay vigilant.

articleHeadline: Monsoon And Diabetes: Why Infection Risk Increases During The Rainy Season
articleSummary: India faces heightened infection risk during monsoon for people with diabetes. Hyperglycaemia weakens neutrophil function, reducing migration, pathogen recognition, and killing, raising risks of urinary tract infections (nearly 2×), surgical-site infections (about 1.5×), and bacteraemia (2–3×). Glycosuria feeds urinary bacteria, notably E. coli, promoting biofilms and colonization; impaired insulin signaling in kidneys can also blunt antibacterial defenses independently of glucose. Rain fosters warmth and humidity, and prolonged wet skin and footwear enable fungal infections—athlete’s foot, ringworm, and jock itch—and diabetic foot ulcers that can progress to infection or gangrene. UTIs may ascend to pyelonephritis; rare invasive mucormycosis is reported in poorly controlled diabetes. Prevention during the season emphasizes thorough drying of the feet, careful foot care, and prompt wound treatment.

articleHeadline: Takeda, Dr Reddy's enter distribution agreement for QDENGA dengue vaccine in India
articleSummary: QDENGA dengue vaccine will be available in India's private market for paediatric and adult vaccination in the first half of 2027, subject to local authority processes. Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India Pvt Ltd and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories have signed a distribution agreement designating Dr. Reddy's as exclusive promoter and distributor in India's private market; Takeda retains rights to promote/distribute QDENGA in the public market and maintains ownership and medical/brand oversight. CDSCO approved QDENGA in July 2026 for ages 4–60, making it India's first approved dengue vaccine. India faces dengue as a public-health challenge, with cases increasing 11-fold over two decades. ICMR surveillance shows all four serotypes co-circulating; 1 in 14 patients are infected with multiple serotypes. Since 2022, Takeda's dengue vaccine has been approved in 43 countries including India, with over 32 million doses distributed. Parliamentary Committee on Health recommended considering dengue vaccine for the Universal Immunization Program.
